extracted.intended_audience: architects, artists, art historians, and informed travelers studying Venetian/Gothic/Renaissance architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for judging Venetian Gothic and Renaissance architecture, ornamentation, and decorative color — emphasizing honesty of materials, workmanship, color principles, and the relation of painting to masonry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value invention and 'soul' over mere method and finish
rubrics_metrics.description: The main mistake of the Renaissance was the unwholesome demand for perfection at any cost; taking the method and finish of great masters as the thing to be copied by common workmen led to loss of the workman's 'soul' and invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer works where invention and 'fire' come first (as in great men like Verrocchio, Ghiberti, Leonardo, Michael Angelo) over pieces that are merely technical copies. Anti-pattern: requiring common workmen to become copyists, producing inanimate, base, or merely technically accomplished work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish works by great masters from meaner imitative work
rubrics_metrics.description: "When it has been done by a truly great man... nothing is more exquisite. But when the cinque-cento work has been done by those meaner men... it is utterly inanimate — a base and helpless copy of more accomplished models; or... a mere accumulation of technical skill."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether quality stems from original conception and life, or from technical execution alone. High technical finish does not substitute for force, invention, or genuine feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty of materials — avoid painted imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The desirableness of ornamentation should be measured by its simple honesty or dishonesty. Painted imitation of woods or marbles is culpable and base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat materials frankly: do not attempt to make marble look like something else by painting. Anti-patterns: faux-marble, faux-wood, or other spurious decorative imitations that deceive the eye and trade on falsehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use marble according to its natural purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Marble is providentially distributed and adapted for human use: white marble is evidently meant for sculpture, colored marble for the covering of large surfaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select materials in accordance with their qualities: white marble for carved work; colored marbles for surface decoration. Consider the physical properties Ruskin describes (suitable hardness, malleability, permanence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chequered/diapered backgrounds should function as grounds, not as designs
rubrics_metrics.description: In chequered patterns of the great periods the greatest care is taken to mark that they are grounds of design rather than designs themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not arrange diaper/chequer patterns to occupy symmetrical positions relative to architectural elements. Gothic practice: cut the ground remorselessly, place windows/doors with no regard to pattern lines; often set patterns obliquely to avoid connection with architectural parts. Anti-pattern: modern architects who align pattern parts symmetrically to architecture, making the pattern a principal design element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quartering / reciprocal interference of color
rubrics_metrics.description: A magnificent attribute of the colouring of the period: the union of one color with another by reciprocal interference — carrying pieces of one color into the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose color masses so that a piece of red is carried into the blue and vice versa; this binds unlike colors into a noble whole. Examples: heraldic quarterings, manuscript illumination, glass-painting. Masters exemplifying this principle: Tintoret, Veronese, Turner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper large color masses with chequering and white (Temperance and Purity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Large fields of color destroy brilliancy and must be tempered by chequering with some other color(s) in smaller quantities, mingled with minute portions of pure white.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small interspersed colors and white to subdue the fullness of color without losing the purity of the colors. This principle gives rise to diapered backgrounds in Gothic decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare walls honestly as grounds for painting (stucco confessed and understood)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stucco (or the white ground of fresco) should be confessed and understood as a ground laid on brick precisely as gesso on canvas, to form a ground for receiving colour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use stucco to imitate stone; accept and use the ground as such. Understand the fragility of painted stucco in exposed situations (sea winds cause rapid decay), and that painted surfaces on exteriors will demand frequent restoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of ephemeral placement of pictorial painting on architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: When painting and architecture were united, the decorative chequerings yielded to elaborate pictorial paintings; such edifices ceased to be architectural schools and became large preparations of artists' panels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architectural façades should not merely be enormous canvases for painters; an excess of pictorial decoration reduces the interest of architecture and risks wasting work, as frescoes on exteriors are fugitive. Balance the roles of architect and painter rather than allowing one to usurp the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value consummate workmanship and honesty even in debased style
rubrics_metrics.description: Though some Byzantine-influenced palaces are debased in style, they are consummate in workmanship and unstained in honour: there is no imperfection and no dishonesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study such buildings for excellence in methods (leveling stones, precision of inlaying) and executive perfection, even if their conception lacks the highest architectural qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural variety (perpetual variety) as a virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ducal Palace retains one pure Gothic character, that of perpetual variety: hardly one window or one panel is like another, and this continual change increases apparent size and nobleness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value subtle, continual variation across a façade rather than monotonous repetition; variety can enhance perceived scale and interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making ornament merely accessory symmetrical to architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: A Gothic builder treats ornamental grounds as independent backgrounds and will change patterns wherever regularity might attract the eye; thus ornament should not be made to line up symmetrically with architectural parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure ornament serves as a pictorial ground and resists being subordinated to architectural symmetry. Anti-pattern: disposing pattern parts to occupy certain symmetrical positions with respect to architectural parts (a modern tendency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess color usage: prefer integrated, restrained chromatic decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic palaces used subdued russet grounds quartered with sculptured masses of white and gold, relieved by smaller inlaid fragments of blue, purple, and green; gilding on mouldings and capitals was used sparingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging chromatic decoration, prefer balanced, tempered palettes with thoughtful use of white and gold; beware the later loss of color and the shift to barren stone exteriors which removed chromatic richness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge the ethical dimension of decoration — truthfulness vs falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern decorative systems that unite the meaninglessness of veined marble with the evanescence of fresco complete the harm by falsehood; the policy of honesty is central to good ornamentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate decorative choices against the moral principle of honesty: is the decoration truthful about material, purpose, and permanence? Anti-pattern: systems that are simultaneously deceptive in materiality and ephemeral in execution.
